blocks.content: 1. INTRODUCTION TO AGRICULTURE

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Agriculture forms the backbone of the Indian economy, employing nearly half of the population despite a declining share in national GDP.
Cropping pattern in India is categorized into three seasons: Kharif (Monsoon), Rabi (Winter), and Zaid (Summer).
The Green Revolution of the 1960s, led by Dr. M.S. Swaminathan, boosted food grain production through HYV seeds, synthetic fertilizers, and enhanced irrigation.
Land reforms aimed at social justice involved abolition of the Zamindari system, tenancy reforms, land ceilings, and consolidation of land holdings.
Key modern initiatives include PM-KISAN, PM Fasal Bima Yojana, Soil Health Card, e-NAM, and the Minimum Support Price (MSP) system.

blocks.content:
Agriculture refers to the cultivation of crops and rearing of animals for food, fibre, fuel and other products.
It is the oldest economic activity and forms the foundation of human civilization.
India is called an agrarian economy because a large proportion of its population depends on agriculture for livelihood.
Even today, agriculture plays a crucial role in employment generation, food security, rural development and industrial growth.
Though the share of agriculture in India’s GDP has declined to around 15–18%, it still employs nearly 45–50% of the population.
This indicates low productivity in the agricultural sector and the need for modernization.
2. IMPORTANCE OF AGRICULTURE IN INDIAN ECONOMY

1. Source of Food:
Agriculture ensures availability of food grains, vegetables, fruits and pulses.
2. Employment Generation:
Nearly half of India's population depends directly or indirectly on agriculture.
3. Contribution to GDP:
Agriculture contributes around 15–18% to India’s GDP.
4. Raw Material for Industries:
Cotton, sugarcane, jute, oilseeds supply raw materials to industries.
5. Export Earnings:
Tea, coffee, spices, rice and marine products contribute to foreign exchange.
6. Rural Development:
Agriculture supports rural income, transport, storage and marketing.
7. Food Security:
Ensures stability in food supply and controls inflation.
3. TYPES OF FARMING IN INDIA
3.1 Subsistence Farming

Subsistence farming is practiced to meet the needs of the farmer and his family.
Characteristics:
• Small land holdings
• Traditional tools
• Low productivity
• Dependence on monsoon
• Little or no surplus for sale
3.2 Commercial Farming

Commercial farming is carried out on a large scale to sell produce in the market.
Features:
• Large land area
• Use of modern machinery
• Use of HYV seeds and fertilizers
• High productivity
• Market-oriented
3.3 Plantation Farming

Plantation farming involves cultivation of a single crop on large estates.
Examples:
Tea, Coffee, Rubber, Sugarcane
Features:
• Capital intensive
• Scientific management
• Labour intensive
• Export oriented
4. CROPPING SEASONS IN INDIA
4.1 Kharif Crops
Agriculture remains the backbone of the Indian economy.

Sown: June–July
Harvested: September–October
Examples:
Rice, Cotton, Maize, Jowar, Bajra
Depend on monsoon rainfall.
4.2 Rabi Crops

Sown: October–November
Harvested: March–April
Examples:
Wheat, Gram, Barley, Mustard
Require cool climate and irrigation.
4.3 Zaid Crops

Grown between Kharif and Rabi seasons.
Examples:
Watermelon, Cucumber, Vegetables
Require irrigation.
5. IRRIGATION IN INDIA

Irrigation is the artificial supply of water to crops.
It reduces dependence on monsoon and increases productivity.
Sources of Irrigation:
• Canals
• Wells and Tube wells
• Tanks
• River valley projects
• Drip irrigation
• Sprinkler irrigation
Importance:
• Ensures regular water supply
• Increases cropping intensity
• Prevents crop failure
• Supports HYV seeds

blocks.content: 6. GREEN REVOLUTION

The Green Revolution was introduced in the 1960s to increase food grain production.
It was led by Dr. M.S. Swaminathan in India.
Key Features:
• High Yielding Variety (HYV) seeds
• Chemical fertilizers
• Irrigation facilities
• Mechanisation
• Multiple cropping
Achievements:
• Increased food grain production
• Made India self-sufficient
• Reduced imports
• Increased rural income
Limitations:
• Regional imbalance
• Environmental degradation
• Soil fertility loss
• Excessive use of chemicals
7. LAND REFORMS IN INDIA

Land reforms were introduced to ensure social justice and improve productivity.
Major reforms:
• Abolition of Zamindari
• Tenancy reforms
• Ceiling on land holdings
• Consolidation of holdings
8. AGRICULTURAL MARKETING

Agricultural marketing includes storage, transportation and sale of agricultural produce.
Problems:
• Lack of storage
• Middlemen exploitation
• Price fluctuation
Reforms:
• APMC Act
• e-NAM
• MSP system
9. GOVERNMENT INITIATIVES

• PM-KISAN Yojana
• PM Fasal Bima Yojana
• Soil Health Card
• Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchai Yojana
• National Food Security Mission
• e-NAM
10. PROBLEMS OF INDIAN AGRICULTURE

• Dependence on monsoon
• Fragmented land holdings
• Low mechanisation
• Farmer indebtedness
• Climate change
• Low income

items: The Green Revolution in India began in the 1960s under the leadership of Dr. M.S. Swaminathan, with Punjab and Haryana being its major beneficiaries.
Minimum Support Price (MSP) is announced by the Government of India to ensure price stability for farmers.
Kharif crops (e.g., Rice, Cotton) depend heavily on monsoon rains, whereas Rabi crops (e.g., Wheat, Gram) require cool weather and irrigation.
Agriculture continues to employ the maximum population compared to any other sector in India.

blocks.content: 11. FUTURE OF INDIAN AGRICULTURE

• Use of technology and AI
• Organic farming
• Precision agriculture
• Sustainable practices
• Digital agriculture
12. SSC EXAM IMPORTANT POINTS

• Agriculture employs maximum population
• Green Revolution began in 1960s
• MSP announced by government
• Punjab and Haryana major beneficiaries
13. CONCLUSION

Agriculture remains the backbone of the Indian economy.
With reforms, technology and government support, Indian agriculture has the potential to become productive, sustainable and globally competitive.
